steps.body: Weekly allowances (dollars): 10, 12, 12, 14, 14, 16, 18, **64**. The 64 is a lone outlier past a huge gap. Mean: 160 ÷ 8 = **20** — larger than seven of the eight allowances! Median: (14 + 14) ÷ 2 = **14**, right among the pack. The shape you see decides the summary you trust: **outliers or skew → median (and IQR); symmetric → mean works fine**.
See how far the mean drifted.

widget.prompt: Allowances 10, 12, 12, 14, 14, 16, 18, 64. The mean is 20. How many of the eight values sit BELOW the mean?

commonErrors.feedback: Half-below is what a MEDIAN promises. The outlier dragged the mean to 20, so 10, 12, 12, 14, 14, 16, and 18 — seven values — all sit below it.
Not quite all — the 64 sits above the mean of 20. The other seven values fall below it.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Only the 64 exceeds 20; the other seven allowances sit below the mean — a 'typical value' describing almost nobody.

predict.prompt: The mean allowance is 20, but one value is 64. Can MOST of the values sit BELOW the mean?

options.label: Yes — one big value lifts the mean
No — half must sit each side
No value can be below the mean

predict.reveal: The mean balances totals, not headcounts — a single 64 hoists it above nearly everyone. Half-on-each-side is the MEDIAN's promise, not the mean's.

explanationVariants: Halves 10, 12, 12, 14 and 14, 16, 18, 64 give Q1 = 12 and Q3 = 17: IQR = 5. The 64 sits outside the fences, so the middle half stays honest.

widget.prompt: Same allowances. Q1 = 12 and Q3 = 17. What is the IQR?

commonErrors.feedback: 54 is the RANGE (64 − 10) — the outlier owns that number. The IQR uses the fences: 17 − 12 = 5.
29 adds the quartiles (17 + 12). The IQR is their difference: 17 − 12 = 5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 17 − 12 = 5 dollars — tiny next to the outlier-driven range of 54.

steps.body: The summaries travel in **pairs**. The mean and range both feel every extreme — use them together on **symmetric, outlier-free** data, where they're honest and familiar. The median and IQR both read positions, not sizes — the **resistant pair** for **skewed or outlier-carrying** data. Mixing (say, median with range) half-fixes the problem: the range still hands the outlier the microphone.

widget.prompt: Drag each data set to the summary pair that should report it.

items.label: Allowances with one $64 outlier
items.feedback: An outlier is exactly what the resistant pair is for — the mean (20) already sits above 7 of the 8 values.

items.label: Trip times: symmetric, no outliers
items.feedback: Symmetric and clean — the mean lands on the median anyway, so the familiar pair serves well.

items.label: House prices with one mansion
items.feedback: The mansion drags the mean and owns the range; report the median and the IQR instead.

items.label: Heights of 20 sixth-graders, evenly bunched
items.feedback: Evenly bunched with no extremes — nothing here to resist; mean + range describe it honestly.

widget.missFeedback: Scan the SHAPE first: any outlier or long tail → the resistant pair (median + IQR); balanced and clean → mean + range.
widget.successFeedback: Assigned — shape first, summaries second. That's the professional habit.

explanationVariants: 'Typical' should describe the pack. The median 14 sits among the seven clustered allowances; the mean 20 describes nobody — it's beyond every value except the outlier itself.
Resistant beats dragged: with the 64 in play, only the median stays with the crowd.

widget.prompt: For the allowances 10, 12, 12, 14, 14, 16, 18, 64 — which number honestly answers 'what's a TYPICAL allowance?'

options.label: The median, 14 — it sits inside the actual cluster
options.feedback: Right — 14 lands among the pack the word 'typical' points at; the outlier can't move it.

options.label: The mean, 20 — it accounts for every dollar
options.feedback: Accounting for every dollar is precisely how the 64 dragged it to 20 — above seven of the eight kids. For 'typical', the resistant median (14) is the honest pick.

options.label: The maximum, 64 — the most impressive value
options.feedback: The 64 is the OUTLIER — the least typical value in the set. Typical means the middle of the pack: the median, 14.

hints: Where does the actual cluster sit?
Which summary can the 64 not touch?

explanationVariants: Mean well ABOVE median is the fingerprint of a high tail or high outlier — big values feed the sum, dragging the mean up while the median holds position.
You've seen the pattern from both sides now: allowances (20 vs 14) and pack weights (10 vs 6.5) — both dragged from above.

widget.prompt: A data set you HAVEN'T seen reports mean 20 and median 14. What does the gap suggest about its shape?

options.label: A high outlier or long high tail is pulling the mean up
options.feedback: That's the fingerprint — a mean sitting well above the median means large values are feeding the sum.

options.label: A low outlier is pulling the mean down
options.feedback: A low outlier would drag the mean BELOW the median. This mean sits above it — the pull comes from large values.

options.label: The data must be perfectly symmetric
options.feedback: Symmetric data puts mean and median together (the trip data had both at 15). A 6-point gap means the data leans — high side.

hints: Which summary gets dragged, and which resists?
The mean sits above the median here.
What kind of values drag a mean UP?

explanationVariants: Mean 20 minus median 14 leaves a gap of 6 dollars — the size of the outlier's distortion of 'typical.'
The two centers should roughly agree on clean data; here they split by 20 − 14 = 6, all of it the 64's doing.

widget.prompt: For the allowances, the mean is 20 and the median is 14. How large is the gap between the two centers?

commonErrors.feedback: 34 is mean + median (20 + 14). The gap is their difference: 20 − 14 = 6.
50 is the outlier minus the median (64 − 14). The question compares the two CENTERS: 20 − 14 = 6.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Gap = mean − median = 20 − 14 = 6 dollars — the outlier's signature.

takeaways: Outliers or skew → the resistant pair: median + IQR.
Symmetric, clean data → mean + range serve honestly (and mean ≈ median anyway).
A mean far from the median is itself evidence: something is dragging it.
steps.teaser: final lesson: run the ENTIRE pipeline — question to plot to summary — on one fresh data set.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Outlier in the data → trust the median.** For 2, 3, 4, 91 the mean is 25 (dragged by the 91) but the median is 3.5, still with the pack.

explanationVariants: The 91 feeds the sum, so the mean (25) leaves the pack; the median (3.5) reads positions and stays.
Resistant summaries ignore sizes: the middle pair is 3 and 4 no matter how big the 91 grows.

widget.prompt: Data: 2, 3, 4, 91. Mean = 25, median = 3.5. Which center better describes a TYPICAL value?

options.label: The median, 3.5
options.feedback: Yes — 3.5 sits inside the 2-to-4 pack; the 91 can't move it.

options.label: The mean, 25
options.feedback: 25 is bigger than three of the four values — the 91 dragged it out of the pack. The resistant median, 3.5, is the honest 'typical.'

options.label: They're equally good
options.feedback: On clean data they'd agree, but here they split 25 vs 3.5 — the outlier broke the tie, and the median is the one still with the pack.
